Incomplete Nature: How Mind Emerged from Matter

Terrence W. Deacon
As physicists work toward completing a theory of the Universe and biologists unravel the molecular complexity of life, a glaring incompleteness in this scientific vision becomes apparent. The “Theory of Everything” that appears to be emerging includes everything but us: that is the feelings, meanings, consciousness, and purposes that make us (and many of our animal cousins) what we

...

y accepting what other theories try to deny: that, although mental contents do indeed lack these material-energetic properties, they are still entirely products of physical processes and have an unprecedented kind of causal power that is unlike anything that physics and chemistry alone have so far explained. It turns out that it is—paradoxically—the intrinsic incompleteness of these semiotic and teleological phenomena that is the source of their unique form of physical influence in the world. Incomplete Nature meticulously traces the emergence of this special causal capacity from simple thermodynamics to self-organizing dynamics to living and mental dynamics, and demonstrates how specific absences (or constraints) play the critical causal role in the organization of physical processes that generate these properties.
